paras: The Gold Park mining camp siege was a mob attack in late November or early December 1881 at the Gold Park mining camp near Leadville, Colorado, in which a crowd besieged a discharged blacksmith named Bayley (also printed Bagley), accused of killing the company foreman, and blew up his cabin with giant powder. Bayley was found dead in the ruins with a bullet wound through the heart, which the original dispatch attributed to suicide, although some later news briefs said the mob had blown him up. Carried on a single Leadville dispatch, the story ran in papers across the country as an example of Western lawlessness.

The Gold Park Mining Company employed Harry Weston as foreman and a man named Turney as superintendent at its camp near Leadville. Bayley was described only as a "discharged blacksmith," with no reason given for his dismissal or the shooting. None of the reports gave the race of Bayley, Weston, or the members of the mob.

According to the dispatch, Bayley shot and killed Weston and then tried without success to shoot Superintendent Turney. The dispatch dated the shooting "four days" earlier, about November 29 by its Denver dateline of December 3, while an Ohio weekly gave "the 30th ult." and a Nevada weekly "last Thursday."

Bayley then fortified himself in his cabin, which was "immediately surrounded by a mob," and the besiegers spent eight hours without dislodging him. Finally a large quantity of giant powder was placed near the door and ignited, and the explosion tore the cabin to pieces. In the ruins Bayley was found with a bullet hole through his heart, "having evidently committed suicide," in the words of the dispatch.

Bayley's sympathizers then threatened Turney's life, and a strong guard was kept around the superintendent's cabin day and night. The camp's "vigilantes," also called "the committee," ordered Jack White and Bayley's other friends out of camp. These "Bayleyites" paraded the town all day with cocked revolvers looking for the vigilantes but left at night, and the dispatch closed with the words "Much trouble is anticipated." No report of an inquest, an arrest, or any official action against the mob appears in the coverage.

The story reached the national press as a Leadville special to the Denver Tribune, which appeared on December 4 in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, the Salt Lake Herald and the Chicago Daily Tribune. Their headlines framed it as frontier disorder rather than as a lynching: "Leadville Lawlessness" in Cheyenne, "Good Times in Leadville" in Salt Lake City, and "Looking for Vigilantes" in Chicago. On December 5 the New-York Tribune headed it "A Fatal Quarrel in a Mining Camp," while the Savannah Morning News called Bayley "A Desperado" and his death "His Desperate Suicide." The next day the Memphis Daily Appeal ran it as "A Murderer Blown Up With Giant Powder" and the Dallas Daily Herald as "A Wild Western Scene."

On its editorial page the Dallas Daily Herald called the affair a "characteristic red-hot Western item" and remarked that it took "dynamite or giant powder to reach him" and that "with its useful efficacy under such circumstances it reached him." Weekly news digests through mid-December cut the story to a sentence or two, and several dropped the suicide. A Maryland paper said that "a murderer was blown up with giant powder in his cabin by a mob," and a Louisiana paper wrote that he had fortified himself "to escape being lynched." An Ohio digest kept the suicide but added that "Partisans of the dead will continue the war." The item was still circulating on December 21 in the Abbeville Press and Banner of South Carolina, which described the besiegers as "a crowd."

Accounts differed on how Bayley died: the full dispatch said he was found shot through the heart and had "evidently" killed himself, while one-line briefs in Maryland and Louisiana papers described him as blown up by the mob. The briefs read as abridgments of the same dispatch rather than independent reports. The surname was printed "Bagley" in the versions datelined Denver and "Bayley" in those datelined Leadville, December 5.

bases: A mob besieged an accused killer in his cabin for eight hours and blew it up with giant powder, a mob attempt on his life after the shooting of a mine foreman (A1, A14, A27).

A mob acting without any reported legal authority besieged and blew up the cabin of a man accused of killing a foreman, and he died; but the full dispatch says he was found shot through the heart, 'evidently' a suicide, while only abridged briefs say the mob blew him up (A1, A14, A26, A27). No report gives the race of anyone involved (A1, A31).

Every account traces to one Leadville special to the Denver Tribune, reprinted in two datelines (Denver Dec. 3/4, Leadville Dec. 5) and later abridged in digests; no local or independent report was found (A1, A4, A14, A31).
